1:
The surname is argued over first. Gill reports that some derive it from Mareshah, a city in Judah, but prefers Moresheth, which he distinguishes from Moresheth-gath; some take the two towns for one, though Jerome shews them different, and knew the place in his own day as a small village near Eleutheropolis. Gill also notes a version reading Micah the son of Morathi, which makes the word a father's name, and refuses it. Clarke places the village in the same neighbourhood. Keil and Delitzsch takes him as sprung from Moresheth-gath in the plain of Judah, and says the epithet distinguishes him from the elder prophet Micah the son of Imlah and from the other ten of the name in the older scriptures. Ellicott draws a contrast: unlike Joel, who identifies himself by his father's name, Micah introduces himself by his native village. On the name itself he, Henry and Keil and Delitzsch agree that it is a shortened Micaiah, meaning who is like Jehovah; Ellicott adds that it was not uncommon but chiefly famous through the earlier Micaiah who withstood Ahab a hundred and fifty years before, and Clarke notes that some have confounded the two men. Henry gives a practical reason for naming the place, that any one might enquire there and find such a person had lived there and was reputed a prophet.

How long the ministry ran is computed three ways. Clarke says fifty years. Calvin thinks it probable the office was discharged for thirty years, possibly more than forty, reckoning sixteen years for the first of the three reigns and as many for the second, and allowing that he may have served to the death of the third king or beyond. Wesley makes the total forty-six, and says the prophet survived the captivity of Israel by ten years. Calvin explains why the dating matters: without it the sermons would be useless, or at least frigid, since knowing the time lets us compare what is alike and different in the men of that age and our own, and view our own life as in a mirror. Henry insists on the other half of the heading, that the word is a divine revelation, to be received not as the word of dying men, which we may judge, but as the word of the living God, by which we must be judged; and that the prophet saw the things he foretold as certainly as if they had been accomplished.

The summons that follows raises a question of audience. Gill takes the people addressed for the nations of Israel, so called from their several tribes, though some understand the rest of the inhabitants of the earth; he cites a Jewish expositor for the wonderfulness of the Hebrew phrase, which strikes the mind like a crier in court calling for silence. Clarke narrows it further, that the word rendered earth should be translated land, only the country of the Hebrews being meant. Calvin widens it instead: the prophet is not content with a calm manner of speaking but rises into an elevated style, and addresses not his own nation only but the whole world; the vehemence shews he already knew the stubbornness of almost all classes before addressing one word to them, since otherwise he would have used mildness and led them rather than driven them. Wesley reads the second clause as an appeal to the senseless creatures, or a summons calling them in as evidence. Ellicott observes that the threefold repetition of the appeal seems to mark the three divisions of the book, and he and Gill both notice that the words are those with which the earlier Micaiah ended his appeal to Ahab. On the last clause Ellicott takes the holy temple for heaven, the Lord's throne being there; Clarke takes it of the temple still standing at Jerusalem, where God remained their king and judge; Wesley allows either.
3:
Which place God goes forth from is disputed. Gill takes it of heaven, where his throne is prepared and his court kept, and is careful that no local motion is meant, since God is everywhere; the going forth signifies not change of place but of dispensation, a removing, as one Jewish expositor has it, from the throne of mercies to the throne of judgment, so that God exercises judgment, his strange work, instead of the mercy he delights in. Wesley says the same in fewer words, that he comes forth as a judge to hear, determine and punish, from heaven. Calvin considers and rejects a third reading, that the temple would hereafter be deprived of God's presence and so become profane, on the model of the vision in which an earlier prophet saw God leave his temple; that sense, he says, does not suit the context. He notes that many take the place for heaven, and that the word descend seems to point that way, but observes that the temple itself stood on a high and elevated spot, so there is nothing inconsistent in saying God descended from it to chastise Judea as it deserved. On his reading the going forth is no desertion of the sanctuary but the opposite, God leaving the temple to ascend his tribunal and prove that he is judge, having been very daringly despised.

The treading down is a picture, not a report. Clarke fills out the figure as a campaign: God is a mighty conqueror issuing from his pavilion and stepping from mountain to mountain, the mountains rushing down and filling the valleys before him, a consuming fire blending all in universal confusion; he does himself what other conquerors do by the multitude of their hosts, levelling mountains, filling some valleys and digging in others for water, and pouring it from hills and dales for the armies by pipes and aqueducts. Wesley takes the treading more narrowly, of trampling under foot all that is high and excellent and matter of their glorying. Gill refuses a literal reading of the melting: the mountains are the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, and the kings and great men in them who lifted their heads as high and thought themselves as secure as mountains, whose hearts would melt through fear when the judgments fell, so that their greatness departed and they were levelled with the meanest subject.

Where the imagery comes from is answered two ways. Ellicott takes it from the giving of the law, where the hills melted like wax at the presence of the Lord of the whole earth. He then reports a writer who refers the same imagery to the memorable earthquake named at the opening of a contemporary prophet, and quotes him: mountains and valleys cleft asunder and melting as in a furnace, the earth heaving like the rising waters of the Nile, the sea bursting over the land, the ground shaking until its solid framework reels to and fro like a drunkard.

Calvin closes with a point of arrangement the versions had missed. The two comparisons do not refer to the same thing: the wax belongs to the mountains and the waters to the valleys, an order common in Hebrew. One old version, not apprehending the sense and finding the result incongruous, tried to reconcile it by transferring the shaking to the mountains and the melting to the valleys, quite contrary to the meaning of the words. On the last line he records renderings that make the place a precipice or a declivity, and gives his own version, that the mountains shall dissolve under him and the valleys burst open, like wax before the fire and waters rolling down a declivity; the verb rendered burst is the word used of water breaking from a fountain, of the young emerging from the egg, and of light dispelling darkness.
5:
The verse is the ground of everything before it. Gill says the calamities signified by those metaphorical phrases did not come by chance, but by the righteous judgment of God for their manifold sins, and especially their idolatry. Calvin makes the same point against a complaint he expects: God is not angry for nothing, though when he appears rigid men clamour as if he were cruel, so the prophet states distinctly that there was a just cause. By naming both houses he means that impiety had prevailed everywhere, no part of the people untainted and no corner of the land able to plead an excuse for its defection; God would be judge of them all and spare neither small nor great.

The two questions that follow are borrowed speech. Calvin says the prophet does not ask for his own satisfaction but repeats, by way of imitation, what he knew was always on their lips, that the charge assumes a false principle and does them a grievous wrong; hypocrites thought themselves pure and were ready to contend with any prophet who reproved them, so he takes their question and answers it. He also notes whom the answer strikes. The prophet does not contend with the common people but attacks the first men; sometimes the common people degenerate while some integrity remains among the higher orders, but here the diseases among the people belonged to the principal men. He names the two chief cities because their inhabitants supposed themselves safe though the whole country were destroyed, relying on their strength and dazzled by empty splendour; such arrogance could not be subdued except by sharp and severe words. What remains, he asks, when kings and their counsellors tread under foot all regard for what is just?

Whether the cities are the sin or its source is put differently. Wesley reads the interrogative as a who rather than a what: who is the spring and cause of that overflowing transgression, and who the cause of the high places? He answers with the capitals, the northern where the kings resided and worshipped idols and set an example to that kingdom, the southern holding the same influence over its own people. Ellicott says the corruption of the country came from the capitals, one on her hill setting an example of idolatry, drunkenness and all the evils of a most profligate society, while even the city set on a hill gave a home in the temple of Jehovah to heathen deities. Clarke says both chief cities were infected, each with its high places and idol worship set against the worship of the true God, and notes that idolatry was practised by the elders even in the temple, so when the royal cities gave the example it was no wonder it spread.

Calvin is careful about what kind of sin is named. The prophet is not reproving gross crimes but perverted forms of worship, as the second clause about the high places makes clearer. It might seem unjust to charge with sin the worship in which men laboriously exercised themselves to pacify God; but God regards as nothing whatever men blend with his worship out of their own heads, so no sin is more detestable than the caprice with which idolaters are inflamed when they observe forms of worship they invented. Calvin then distinguishes the two kingdoms as they stood. The northern had so fallen as to be altogether degenerate, nothing visible among them having any affinity to the true and legitimate worship of God, while the southern had retained some form of religion, but with a mixture of superstitions in it. The prophet pronounces the same sentence on both, since God allows nothing from the inventions of men to be joined to his word; there was no less sin on the high places of the one land than in the abominations dominant in the other.
6:
The heap and the vineyard are explained three ways. Gill offers a field ploughed and laid in heaps, or stones gathered out of a field and a planted vineyard and thrown into a pile, so the city becomes a heap of stones and rubbish; he ascribes the doing of it to God, who instigated the Assyrian king and whose providence prospered the besieging army. Calvin gives the same image from the husbandman's side, that the ruins would differ nothing from the heaps of the fields, since men who find stones in their fields throw them into a corner out of the way. Wesley takes the figure from the planting rather than the clearing, that in making vineyards they dig up the earth and cast it into hillocks, and the city would be made like that. Ellicott takes it neither of stones nor of hillocks but of the site: the city was to be reduced to what it had been before the days of Ahab, the palatial city of the northern kings returning to the vineyard it was before its hill was sold to the founder of the dynasty; and the fruitfulness of those vines, he adds, suggests one cause of its ruin, quoting the woe on the crown of pride and the drunkards on the head of the fat valleys. Clarke reports one writer for the same observation, that the city stood on a hill, the right soil for a vineyard.

The second half of the threat is read alike. Wesley notes that the city was built on a high hill with a deep valley beneath, so the stones could be poured down; he and Clarke both take the discovering of the foundations to mean that walls, fortifications and public buildings would be razed to the ground.

On the images Calvin is careful about what the anger falls on. God mentions the idols expressly so the people might understand why they were so severely punished, the cause being that they had abandoned themselves to ungodly forms of worship and departed from the law. God is not angry with stones and wood, he says, but observes the abuse of them, when men pollute themselves by wickedly worshipping such things. Gill turns to the fate of the images, beaten to pieces by the Assyrian army for the gold and silver of which they were made or adorned, as conquerors usually treated the gods of nations they subdued, and this took in not only the images at the capital but those in all the other cities that fell.

The hires divide the readers. Clarke takes them literally: multitudes of women gave the money they gained by public prostitution at the temples toward the support of the priesthood and the ornamenting of walls, altars and images, so that these things, and perhaps several of the images themselves, were literally the hire of harlots; God threatens to deliver the whole to enemies who would spend it as it was acquired, so that to the hire of a harlot these things should return. Ellicott reads the word as metaphor: the falling away from loyalty to God is compared by the prophets to a wife deserting her husband, and these hires are the offerings made at the shrines of the idols to which the people had transferred their worship, all of which the Assyrians would carry off to adorn their own temples. Wesley agrees, taking them for the rich gifts given to the idols by deceived worshippers, turned by the conquerors to the service of other idols. Calvin notes that the word is properly a gift or present, and that repeating it stamps with disgrace all the wealth of the city; the reproach is that they had heaped together great riches after the manner of harlots, and he traces the arrangement to the king who constructed a new form of worship to secure his own kingdom.
8:
Why the prophet mourns in person is explained. Calvin says he assumes the character of a mourner to impress a people almost insensible in their torpor: it was necessary to bring them to view the scene itself, that seeing their destruction they might be touched with grief and fear. Lamentations of this kind are everywhere in the prophets, and Calvin turns the point on the reader, that we are not much unlike that people, remaining quiet in our filth however God terrifies us. He distinguishes two cases: the prophets sometimes assumed mourning and sometimes felt real grief, and when they spoke of aliens they lamented without really grieving, transferring the sorrows of others to themselves in order to persuade men. Henry makes the prophet chief mourner in a long train attending the funeral of a ruined kingdom, and gives two reasons: partly to mollify the predictions and shew the judgments were not denounced out of ill-will, the prophets dreading the woeful day more than anyone; and partly to shew how dreadful the calamities would be and stir up a holy fear, that by repentance the people might turn away wrath. He adds that we ought to lament the punishments of sinners as well as the sufferings of saints.

The stripping is described from the wardrobe. Gill takes it of putting off the upper garment, the rough one the prophets wore, and notes that in such cases they sometimes rent their clothes and sometimes walked naked, as an earlier prophet did; the word rendered stripped, say the Jewish commentators, carries the sense of a man bereft of his senses, who goes about without his clothes. Wesley says the same more briefly, as one who in bitterness of passion has cast off his upper garment.

The two creatures are identified alike. Ellicott says they are literally jackals and ostriches, chosen for the dismal howls and screeches they make at night; Henry calls them ravenous beasts that meet in the night, Wesley beasts that haunt desolate places. Clarke reports a rendering giving jackals and the daughters of the ostrich, and adds that the howlings of the one by night are most lamentable, while the other is remarkable for its shrieking and groaning after nightfall, one traveller saying he had often heard them groan as if in the greatest agonies.

What is said of the wound divides them. Gill renders it that her stroke is desperate, the ruin inevitable because the decree was gone forth and the people hardened, so that they were not restored and are not to this day. Clarke and Ellicott read it the same way, that nothing shall prevent utter ruin and the city is incurable. Calvin refuses that sense outright: the word means properly full of grief, and though others render it desperate or incurable, that meaning does not suit this place. He adds a textual note, that the true reading is the singular, her wound, and that although only two manuscripts have it, the preceding participle and the following verbs are singular, and one old version has the singular too.

How far the blow reaches is the last question. Calvin observes that the prophet says first to Judah, naming the land, then confines it to the cities, since closed gates ordinarily force an enemy to stop; the point is that they would be no hindrance, the enemy coming to the very gates and to the chief city itself. Ellicott reads the clause more mildly, that the outlying towns shudder at the invader's advance while the capital itself is spared. Clarke sets the kingdoms in order, the captivity of the north first and the south after; Wesley takes what comes to be the contagion of her sins and the indignation of God against it. Keil and Delitzsch marks the transition: the judgment penetrating the southern kingdom is depicted by an individualising enumeration of the cities to be smitten.
10:
The opening prohibition is a quotation. Ellicott says the prophet lets his lament flow after the strain of an older elegy that told the news not in Gath; Gill says the phrase is borrowed from that place and the reason given there holds here. Gill grants that the invasion could not be hidden from the Philistines, but says it was desirable if possible, since the news would be matter of rejoicing to them, and that would aggravate the distress. Clarke puts it as a caution, not to let the prediction be known among them lest they glory over it, and Wesley reads the second clause as an order to make no public weeping. Calvin faces the apparent inconsistency: the prophet has just described a calamity evident to all and now commands silence, yet there is no contradiction, since the evil could not be hidden when a kingdom was desolated and the enemy stood at the gates of the capital. What is described is a feeling rather than a possibility, of men desirous of hiding their disgrace from aliens; it vexes us when enemies taunt us in our misfortunes, and when no hope remains we wish at least to perish in secret, dishonour being often harder to bear than any other evil.

Ellicott adds a conjecture about the second clause. The parallelism seems to require a town name where the English gives at all, and the Hebrew word may, by adding a letter which has dropped out, be read as the coastal city later called Ptolemais and now Acca; one old Greek version accords with that reading. So the parallelism is maintained and the thought completed, that they should not mention the trouble in their enemies' cities but bewail it in their own. Clarke points out the play on words in the next name, that the sense is to roll oneself in the dust in the house of dust, and places the town in Benjamin; Wesley observes that it lay farther from the Philistines.

The towns that follow are located only by conjecture. Gill puts one of them between Eleutheropolis and Ashkelon, reports a writer who identifies it with a city in Galilee and another who takes it for a town named from its ornament, and notes the margin reading thou that dwellest fairly, understood by some of the northern capital. Clarke reports the same two identifications. Ellicott says the sites are conjectural but probably south-west of the capital, the prophet following the march of the invading army; Wesley guesses at the two capitals themselves.

Calvin reads the passage as a series of names turned against their bearers. The first means splendid, so the sense is that though the city is now called beautiful the Lord will discover its shame, and its nakedness will be so great a disgrace that no one would deign to look on it; the correspondence is in the meaning of the words rather than their sound. The second answers to a verb meaning to remove or migrate, so the prophet says the inhabitant will remain quiet at home, contrary to the name, since the place was named from removing and was one of much traffic; though he see his neighbours dragged into exile, he will not dare to stir. On the last clause Calvin says the verb means to stand and the standing is the enemy's station, but notes that interpreters vary, some taking it that the enemy once settled in the land would not depart. Ellicott renders it that the wailing of the third town shall take from you his standing, meaning no support will be found in its inhabitants; he explains the middle clause as saying they remained in their city through fear of the enemy. Wesley reads the standing as the enemy encamping among them and standing on their ground, so they would have no opportunity of coming out to help their neighbours.
12:
What the first town did while it waited turns on a verb. Gill offers three renderings: that the inhabitants waited carefully for good and had the reverse befall them, that though they waited for good they were disappointed, or that they were grieved for good, that is for what they had lost when they saw the capital in distress. Calvin says the verb means to grieve and takes it so, the townsmen grieving for their lost property and former happy condition; but the same verb means to expect, so some approve the other exposition, that they depended in vain on an empty expectation, being doomed to destruction. That view he calls very suitable, since their hope would disappoint them when even the chief city was not exempted; and although God had by a miracle raised the siege of that city through an angel, this town was not able to escape vengeance. He mentions a harsher explanation too, that its citizens were to be debilitated. Ellicott says there are various ways to the interpretation but the result is the same: the people were in distress, grieved at the spoiling of their property and longing for good, while evil was the Lord's decree against the capital. Wesley gives a flood of affliction swallowing up other cities and swelling to the head city, and Keil and Delitzsch marks the same movement, that the judgment will not even stop at the capital but spread further over the land.

The name is discussed apart from the verb. Gill reports one writer who thinks that by a transposition of letters another town is intended, and a second who takes it for a city of the south; the word signifies bitterness, or according to others rough places, and may describe the inhabitants of such places. Clarke notes only that a city of similar name stood in the same tribe.

The command to the next town is to run. Ellicott glosses it that they must make haste and escape with their goods; Wesley that they must fly from the enemy's sword; Calvin that it would not be safe to remain, and nothing better than to flee elsewhere with their substance: think of flight, and of the quickest. What beast is meant is another matter. Gill canvasses horses, camels, dromedaries and mules, and dwells on the dromedary, which an old writer calls a lesser and swifter sort of camel able to go a hundred miles in a day, what the Jewish writers call a flying camel because it runs as a bird flies, where an ordinary camel makes thirty. Calvin says the word is of uncertain meaning and some render it swift horses; whatever the animal, there would be no time for flight unless they made great haste. Keil and Delitzsch simply renders it harness the horse to the chariot.

Why this town is called the beginning of sin is answered from its position. Clarke says the words seem to intimate it was the first city of the south to receive the idolatrous worship of the north. Ellicott says the same from its being a border city, which made it the channel for the idolatry set up in the north, and adds its standing: the most important of the cities named here, fortified by one king, sought as a refuge by another fleeing a conspiracy, and left at the end as one of the last two defenced cities of the south. Calvin agrees that its citizens were the first to embrace those corruptions and depart from the pure worship of God, and that when contagion entered there it crept by degrees into neighbouring places; he notes too that although the daughter of Zion is named, the prophet takes a part for the whole. Wesley says the town, being nearest the idolatrous kingdom, took the infection and conveyed it onward, the transgressions named being not only idolatry but other sins.
14:
What the presents are divides the readers. Gill takes them for tribute sent in distress, gifts going to the Philistines for help against the Assyrians; Wesley says the same. Calvin reads it as an attempt to pacify the enemy and redeem themselves and their neighbours, and says the prophet enumerates such particulars so the hand of God might be more evident when men found what had been predicted come true. Ellicott takes the clause the other way: the town shall cease to give the protection due from a husband to a wife and shall hand her a bill of divorce, the Hebrew word meaning either the presents sent with a daughter or a wife's dismissal.

On the next name the voices agree. Ellicott puts the town on the sea coast between two known ports, says its name means false or deceptive and is used of a river that dries up and disappoints the traveller, and concludes it shall prove a broken reed to the kings who trusted it. Calvin makes the same point from the alliteration, that gifts are sent to the sons of a lie, for a lie, the city having its name from its guiles. Wesley calls it a lying refuge, a prop that will break under them; Clarke supposes a king pressed by an enemy sent to such places for succour. Clarke and Calvin both admire the device. Clarke lists the instances, dust and the town of dust, the town and the swift beast, the town and a lie, and says such plays were reputed ornaments. Calvin says the instances here and in the five verses before are unparalleled elsewhere in the prophets, and that where there is no coincidence of sound there is sometimes a direct contrast of ideas.

The heir is identified without dispute. Gill says the town's name signifies an inheritance, so an heir is announced for it; he rejects the identification of that heir with the Persians and makes it the Assyrian king. Ellicott renders the word rather as the possessor, one who takes by force, and Wesley as the conqueror who possesses by right of conquest. Ellicott adds that it was fortified by one king and was the scene of another's victory over an immense host. Gill notes that many think this the prophet's own birthplace, so his faithfulness appears in declaring God's whole counsel against his own town, which aggravates the sin of inhabitants who had such a prophet and regarded him not. Calvin makes it a rule: the prophet spares not his own kindred, and as God is no respecter of persons his servants ought to deal impartially with all. Of the last town Clarke says only that it was a fenced city towards the Dead Sea, and confesses much obscurity in these closing verses, referring to circumstances no history records. Ellicott identifies it as the place that gave its name to the famous cave of David's refuge, and reads the clause as saying this last refuge of Israel's glory shall be seized by the invader.

The closing summons is to mourning. Gill and Calvin both explain that baldness was made in mourning by plucking or shaving the hair, some taking the first verb, Calvin notes, as pluck or tear off. Calvin prefers children of thy indulgences to darling children, and makes it a reproach, since those delicacies came from God's extreme kindness in long sparing them. On the bird Clarke refers the baldness to the moulting season, when the creature is sickly and its strength exhausted; Ellicott says instead that the Hebrew name covers the kinds of vulture, entire baldness being a marked feature of that bird; Wesley says one species is entirely bald. Clarke reads the captivity as the one under the Assyrian king; Ellicott holds that the terms used of the desolation must mean a more complete calamity than that invasion, suiting rather the later Babylonian captivity.
